seo.title: Tools vs Resources vs Prompts — The Only Question That Matters

seo.description: Tools, resources and prompts differ by one thing only — who pulls the trigger.

scenes.narration: Tools, resources, prompts. People mix them up constantly, and one question tells them apart.

scenes.headline: Who pulls [the trigger]
scenes.caption: the three primitives
scenes.premise: One server, three kinds of thing it can expose. The only question that separates them is who decides when it runs.
scenes.narration: Every MCP server can expose exactly three kinds of thing, and they're told apart by who decides when each one runs. ^A tool is a function Claude chooses to call. Claude reads the description, decides the tool is relevant, and asks for it. The model is in charge. ^A resource is data your own code fetches, because your app decided it needed context — a dropdown that needs filling, a file the user just opened. Your code is in charge. ^And a prompt is a workflow the person triggers, typically by typing a slash command. The user is in charge. Same server, same decorator style — but three different owners, which is why picking the wrong one makes a feature fight you.

cells.label: Tools
cells.sub: functions the model chooses to call

cells.label: Resources
cells.sub: data your code fetches for context

scenes.headline: The same job, [three ways]
scenes.caption: when the answer flips
scenes.premise: One job — 'show me the release notes' — built three different ways. The code is nearly identical; the control is not.
scenes.narration: Here's the test that makes the rule stick. Take one job — show me the release notes — and notice that all three primitives can do it. The code is nearly identical. What changes is who starts it. ^As a tool, Claude decides. You ask a question, Claude reasons that release notes would help, and calls it unprompted. Good when the model should judge relevance. ^As a resource, your app decides. The user opens the releases screen, so your code fetches the notes and puts them in context before anyone asks. Good when you already know they're needed. ^As a prompt, the user decides. They type slash release notes, and your pre-written instruction runs. Good when you want the same careful workflow every time. ^Same data, same server, three different owners — and picking the wrong one shows up as a feature that fires when nobody wanted it, or never fires when everybody did.

cells.label: as a Tool
cells.sub: Claude calls it unprompted, when it judges it relevant

cells.label: as a Resource
cells.sub: your screen opened, so your code fetched it first

cells.label: as a Prompt
cells.sub: they typed /release-notes and got the same careful workflow

cells.label: pick wrong
cells.sub: it fires unasked, or never fires at all

scenes.narration: Ask who is in control, and the primitive names itself. Full course on the channel.
